file_title: File:Bai Tu Long Bay - Quang Ninh - Vietnam (35892945123).jpg

captions.und: Bai Tu Long Bay is a bay in Vietnam. It encompasses Bai Tu Long National Park. Bai Tu Long Bay is northeast of Hạ Long Bay

In traditional Vietnamese culture, the dragon is a powerful and sacred mythical creature. According to legend, Vietnam was constantly fighting off intruders from the north thousands of years ago. The Jade Emperor who ruled heaven (Ngọc Hoàng Thượng đế) sent the Mother Dragon and her children to help defeat the invaders. When the dragons descended, they immediately thwarted an attack in the Eastern Sea, incinerating the enemies with fire and emeralds from their mouths. After the battle, the dragons decided to stay in the mortal world, taking human form to help with farming and expanding the country. Legend says the Mother Dragon landed in what is known today as Hạ Long Bay; her children set down in Bai Tu Long Bay. Some say the emeralds used during the attack were scattered around the waters and formed the islands seen today. The image at the top of this page shows the two bays along the northeast coast of Vietnam, about 170 kilometers (100 miles) east of Hanoi. The image was acquired on November 12, 2020, by the Operational Land Imager (OLI) on Landsat 8. Hạ Long Bay—roughly meaning “descending dragon”—is known for some of the most breathtaking scenery in Vietnam. This World Heritage Site includes about 1,600 islands and islets, most topped with rainforests. Most of the islands are very steep and unhabitable, so tourists explore their edges via boat. Hạ Long Bay includes Bai Tu Long Bay National Park to the northeast. The park contains 40 islands and almost 2,000 species of plants and animals—of which 70 are listed as endangered species. The park spans both land and water, including broad-leaved rainforests, coral reefs, and shallow water areas. The image above shows one of the larger islands of Bai Tu Long Bay National Park. Close to shore, many fishermen practice aquaculture, using cages to raise grouper, cobia, tiger fish, king butler, and other fish. Much of the area around the bays is comprised of limestone, with drowned karst landforms scattered around the waters. In fact, the area contains some the most impressive range of karst formations in the world, allowing researchers to study the geoclimatic history in the area. The karst landforms appear as pillars with different erosional features such as conical peaks, arches, and caves; some are 1,200 meters (4,000 feet) thick. The limestone began forming around 340 million years ago when carbonate sediments from land entered the ocean. Over millions of years, the limestone eventually hardened and thickened into the famous karsts seen today.

artist: NASA Earth Observatory images by Joshua Stevens, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Story by Kasha Patel.

file_title: File:Door carved with dragons, Thần-quang Pagoda, 17th-century.jpg

captions.vi: Door carved with dragons, Thần-quang Pagoda, 17th-century. Width = 242cm, Height = 190cm, Length = 9.5cm. The door was made from iron with wood- engraved dragons, unicorns (two of four sacred animals) and clouds - the common theme of Buddhist art. The object represented the plastic style of the Revival Lê Dynasty in the 17th Century which implied the powerful living force of the Annamese. This is a typical work of art from Annam's classical fine arts period.

captions.vi: Cầu Vát rất thơ mộng soi bóng xuống dòng sông Cầu. Ảnh chụp từ bờ phía Đông nhìn sang phía Hà Nội dọc theo cầu Vát. Cầu Vát nối huyện Sóc Sơn, Hà Nội với huyện Hiệp Hòa, Bắc Giang. Cầu nằm trên Tỉnh lộ 296, chiều dài khoảng 200m, đưa vào sử dụng khoảng năm 2000.
captions.en: Vát Bridge is very poetic architecture and reflects on the Cau River. Photo taken from the east bank looking to Hanoi along the Vat bridge. Vat bridge connects Soc Son district, Hanoi with Hiep Hoa district, Bac Giang. The bridge is located on Provincial Road 296, about 200m in length, put into use in 2000.

captions.en: Exhibit in the Vietnam National Museum of Fine Arts - Hanoi, Vietnam. This artwork is old enough so that it is in the public domain.

Vĩnh Lăng stele (replica). Height: 330 cm, breadth: 280 cm. Stone, erected in the 6th year of Thuận Thiên reign (1433). Early Lê dynasty, ancient capital of Lam Kinh, Thanh Hóa province, central Vietnam. Inscribed by Nguyễn Trãi. Commemorative element. Inscription showed on biography of Lê Lợi, leader of Lam Son uprising (1418-1427) against Ming invaders from China, from beginning to final victory and him becoming the first king of the Early Lê dynasty in 1428. This stele is also one of typical stone sculptures of Vietnam fine art in the 15th century. National Museum of Vietnamese History, Hanoi.

file_title: File:Entre terre et eau (Chau Doc, Vietnam) (6588161767).jpg

captions.und: A la frontière avec le Cambodge, la région de Chau Doc vue depuis le sommet du Mont Sam Le delta du Mékong est le pays de la terre et de l'eau (Dat Nuoc) Le Mont Sam (Nui Sam) haut de 230 m est à 6 Km de Chau Doc. C'est un important lieu de pèlerinage, de nombreux temples ont été construits tout autour du mont. Une grande partie de la région est encore inondée en décembre, comme on peut le constater sur le panorama. Les habitations se regroupent le long des routes, qui sont elles-mêmes construites sur des digues. Cette zone agricole du Vietnam est particulièrement pauvre en raison de la durée de l'inondation qui limite le nombre de récoltes de riz. Les principales ressources de ses habitants viennent du fleuve avec l'élevage des poissons-chats dans des maisons flottantes. Le Cambodge se trouve à gauche sur la photo, Chau Doc est au centre, le Bassac est au fond.

captions.en: Typical scenery of the coastal plains of Thua Thien Hue Province in Central Vietnam, separated from the sea by coastal lagoons and sand bars, including Tam Giang-Cầu Hai Lagoon, pictured here. This lagoon, connected to the mouth of the Perfume River is the largest coastal lagoon in Southeast Asia, with a length of 68 km. The village in the background is Phuoc Tuong Village, located on the road between Da Nang and Hue.

file_title: File:Bares alrededor de la Plaza Dong Kinh Nghia Thuc, Hanoi, Vietnam (36660606041).jpg

captions.und: La Plaza Dong Kinh Nghia Thuc es una pequeña plaza dentro del casco antiguo de Hà Nội, adyacente al lago Hoam Kiem. Luces, colores, sonidos y un flujo continuo de personas y vehículos se unen de manera caótica, dando a la ciudad una vibración vital en cada momento del día. La zona de la plaza se convierte en el lugar donde convergen los puntos de referencia culturales e históricos tales como el lago Hoam Kiem y el distrito de 36 calles donde se encuentra el centro histórico de la ciudad. Es un buen lugar para vivir el "ambiente de Hanoi", pasear, conocer gente local y participar en actividades tradicionales, sobre todo durante las noche de los viernes, en las que las calles se vuelven peatonales.

file_title: File:A 5,000 gal fuel tank truck is backed onto a BARC at Duc Pho.jpg

captions.en: TASK FORCE GALLAGHER A resupply operation supported by a Landing Ship Transport (LST) unit of the U.S. Navy to elements of the 3rd Bde Task Force, 25th Inf Div, and the 1st Bde, 101st Abn Div (Sep). The cooperation was made from the South China Sea utilizing a beachhead at Duc Pho in Quang Ngai Province. A 5,000 gal fuel tank truck of the 1st Log Comd is backed onto a BARC from which it will put out to sea to refuel from a tanker that is anchored off shore. NARA 111-CCV-527-CC40036

Members of Co "C" and the village chief walk through the village of Sa Huynh where a small harbor is being constructed. NARA 111-CCV-230-CC42823

Cao Dai Temple of Saigon, Trần Hưng Đạo, Boulevard, Chợ Quán
Saigon Cao Dai Temple (interior)

The colorful Saigon Holy House is a Caodaist temple. Caodaism (Cao Đài ) is a religion that originated in southern Vietnam in 1921. It was formally organized in 1926. Following the fall of Saigon in 1975, the practice of Caodaism was banned by the communist government. Legal recognition was regained in 1997. The official name of the religion is Great Way of the Third Time of Redemption (Đại Đạo Tam Kỳ Phổ Độ), the first two times having been the early sages such as the Buddhas and Confucius and then Jesus but humanity did not pay sufficient attention. Caodaism theology is a mixture of Confucianism, Taoism, and Mahayana Buddhism plus elements of Vietnamese folk religion (such as ancestor worship) and Roman Catholicism (such as the hierarchy of clergy). Followers of Caodaism number in the millions. On Google Earth: Saigon Holy House 10°45'16.78"N, 106°40'46.23"E

file_title: File:0040423 Thap Binh Lam Cham Hindu temple, Phuoc Hoa, Binh Dinh Vietnam 016.jpg

captions.en: The Thap Binh Lam, also called Kalan Binh Lam, is a 10th century brick tower Hindu temple in Binh Lam village of Tuy Phuoc district, Binh Dinh province Vietnam. It is notable for being among those temples that are midst a village on a natural mound, rather than being on top of a hill. The Thap Binh Lam has a square plan (11.5 meter x 11.5 meter), about 20 meters high with shrinking repetition of the temple motif in the upper storeys. The temple faces east. Bands of the outer walls were carved with Hindu motifs. The original dedication is unclear.

file_title: File:0040423 Thap Canh Tien Cham Hindu temple, Binh Dinh Vietnam 021.jpg

captions.en: The Thap Canh Tien, sometimes called the Dong tower, is a brick-stone composite tower Hindu temple near Nhon Hau commune of An Nhon district, Binh Dinh province Vietnam. It is located about 25 kilometers from Quy Nhon city midst rice farms and forested area on top of a small hill. The Thap Canh Tien is notable for being reasonably well preserved Vijaya era Hindu monument. It faces east and has a square plan. It had a vestibule (antarala) but that is now lost. The sanctum (garbhagriya) is similar to over dozen Champa Hindu sites in and near Quy Nhon. The Thap Canh Tien illustrates the late Champa architecture with Khmer influences. It is notable as among the sites where the design of columns, claddings, artwork, arches can be studied. The temple has been variously dated between 12th to 14th century.

file_title: File:0040423 Thap Duong Long Cham tower temples, Hindu trinity, Binh Dinh Vietnam 003.jpg

captions.en: The Thap Duong Long is a three tower Cham Hindu monuments complex in Tây Sơn district of Bình Định province, Vietnam. The site is much larger than the surviving towers, with excavations revealing the original complex to include a mandapa and other structures. The brick tower temples (kalan) were originally dedicated to the Hindu trinity – Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, as is evidenced by the artwork found at the site. Each tower temple has a square plan, follow the Vijaya style of Hindu architecture vertically and are capped with a ring of amalakas at the top. The Thap Duong Long is from the 12th century. The site, like numerous Buddhist and Hindu sites in Vietnam were badly damaged during the Vietnam war. It was restored in the 2010s, though plants and tree tend to rapidly grow in between the bricks. This site should not be confused with Dong Duong Cham temple site in Quang Nam province. file_title: File:Thap Nhan Hindu temple, Tuy Hoa, Phu Yen province, Vietnam 15.jpg

captions.en: The Thap Nhan or Nhan Tower, sometimes called the Swallow Tower, is a Champa era Hindu temple located on the Nhan hill in Tuy Hoa, near the Da Rang river. It sits on the top of a hill with sweeping views of the city, port and farmlands. The site and the temple has been variously dated to the about the 5th century, 9th century, and 11th century. Given the artwork and style similarities to the Po Nagar temple, it is more likely from the 11th century. The Thap Nhan temple illustrates one of seven styles of Hindu architecture that evolved in Vietnam between the 8th and 16th centuries. It is a uncommon example of a four storey brick temple with a square plan, about 25 meters high. The upper sections of the Nhan Tower are miniature replica of a classic Champa Hindu temple. The Nhan Tower temple was originally dedicated to Uma and Shiva (Parvati–Shiva).

captions.en: The Thap Phu Loc is a brick tower Hindu temple in An Nhon district, Binh Dinh province Vietnam. It is located on the top of a hill, about 40 kilometers from Quy Nhon city midst rice farms and forested area. Visible in the distance from the Thap Canh Tien, it is reachable by a short though steep hike that starts south of the monument. The Thap Phu Loc is an 11th to 12th century Hindu temple with a square plan. It opens to the east. Its architecture is simpler than Thap Canh Tien which is about 4 kilometers away.

file_title: File:0040323 Thap Doi Cham Hindu complex, Quy Nhon, Binh Dinh Vietnam 009.jpg

captions.en: The Thap Doi twin towers are 12th century Cham Hindu temples site located near the coast within the city limits of Quy Nhon, Binh Dinh province of Viet Nam. The site is located near the Ha Thanh river and it originally had three temples. However, the northern tower that was closest to the river collapsed in the 19th-century. The other two stand, were restored and strengthened in the 1990s. The Thap Doi temples reflect the Vietnamese innovations and architecture that developed during the Vijaya period. They incorporate Khmer (Cambodian) interpretations of Hindu architecture. The temples include Garuda figures on corners, suggestive of a thriving Vishnu tradition. Art panels here are eroded being close to sea shore. One of these friezes include an army of monkeys that remind of the Ramayana epic. Another frame shows a praying man in yoga posture. These too are from the 12th century. The main tower now houses a linga and yoni, but this was brought in during the colonial era. There are inscriptions on the door jamb, but the surviving text does not help identify the builder or the deities that were originally worshipped here. The artwork that survives, and the panels from here that are now preserved in the Binh Dinh museum, indirectly suggest that this three tower complex was either dedicated to the Hindu trinity or to the Vishnu tradition.

file_title: File:Another look at the Dong Xuan Market in the Hanoi old quarter (31454085665).jpg

captions.und: Another look at the large Dong Xuan Market market in the Hanoi old quarter. And no, I did not go in, as my driver guide was not very clear in describing the place to me, thanks to the language barrier. He said both market, big, museum. Now market or museum? At any rate, after a long, long day that what started at 05:30 the previous day, followed by a red eye flight, and sleep deprived till 16:00 now, it had been nearly 24hr without sleep, and I was totally pooped, so I simply waved him to move on. At any rate, I still had to find the jeans I mentioned earlier, so that was a mission still not accomplished and which needed looking into. (Hanoi, Vietnam, Oct./ Nov. 2016)

captions.en: One of the gates at the temple. The Temple of Literature ( Van Mieu ), dedicated to Confucius, was founded in 1070 by Emperor Ly Thanh Tong. In 1076, Vietnam's first university was established here to educate Vietnam's administrative and warriors class. Parts of the university date from this earlier time period although the large complex has undergone many changes over the centuries. But recent archaeological study indicates that the architecture of this site belongs primarily to the Ly (1010-1225) and Tran (1225-1400) Dynasties. The complex is in a tranquil park-like site in the heart of central Hanoi. Vietnam

Khuc Van Cac pavilion area. These open pavilions provided space for study and leisure. Thien Quang Tinh pond in front. The Temple of Literature ( Van Mieu ), dedicated to Confucius, was founded in 1070 by Emperor Ly Thanh Tong. In 1076, Vietnam's first university was established here to educate Vietnam's administrative and warriors class. Parts of the university date from this earlier time period although the large complex has undergone many changes over the centuries. But recent archaeological study indicates that the architecture of this site belongs primarily to the Ly (1010-1225) and Tran (1225-1400) Dynasties. The complex is in a tranquil park-like site in the heart of central Hanoi. Vietnam

file_title: File:0040223 My Son Group A, Cham Hindu temples complex, Vietnam 019.jpg

captions.en: Group A is also called Thap Chua. The group includes 19 ruined structures. The Group A monuments were in good state until 1969, when at a time of escalating Vietnam war, the US ordered a B52 bomber to drop numerous bombs on the My Son site. The Group A temples were among those badly damaged and lost to history. Except for the massive stone Shiva linga that survived the bombing, the high temples of My Son A group were destroyed during the war. Henri Parmentier and pre-1960 scholarly publications are now the memories of Group A monuments. Group A have the clearest view of the most sacred mountain of the Cham people. Overview: Mỹ Sơn is one of the largest historic, archaeological and cultural sites in southeast Asia. Now a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Vietnam , it served as a major religious and political center of the Champa Kingdom between the 4th and 14th centuries. My Son site has spiritual roots in 1st–millennium Hinduism whose artistic interpretation evolved with Cham heritage and ideas. My Son sanctuary is located in the Duy Xuyen District of Quang Nam Province, in central Viet Nam. It is set within a valley surrounded by mountains, one of whom resembles the legendary Mount Meru and Kailasha. This is where the sacred Thu Bon river starts, then irrigates one of the heartland of Champa regions before meeting the South China Sea near famed historic port and economic center of Hoi An. My Son is the largest Champa site, whose history can be traced to the Dua people. They, inspired by Hinduism, founded Champapura in late 2nd century (192 CE). These thereafter came to be known as Champa or Cham people. The oldest structures at My Son are from the 4th century. Over time, well over 100 Hindu shrines and structures were built here, mostly to the Shiva tradition – the Cham state religion, but also to Vishnu, Durga, Krishna and others. The site, at times, attracted syncretic Hindu-Mahayana Buddhist ideas. The My Son site is spread over miles, was predominantly built with bricks, and either face east or west. The site is archaeologically studied in many Nhoms (groups) – Group A ithrough Group M. Group B–C–D (Thap Cho) are together, built over 4th to 13th century near the confluence of two major river streams, and form the largest group of shrines. Group E–F (Thap Ho Khe) are also together, dated to about the 7th-century, distinctive for the Vallabhi and Kalan architecture. Group A (Thap Chua) is the most magnificent structures built from 5th century onwards and dedicated to Shiva. Group G, H, L, M are isolated. Many of the isolated sites are rarely visited except by archaeologists and devout Cham pilgrims. The My Son site was in good state of preservation through the colonial era. However, the site was badly damaged in the wars that followed, particularly the Vietnam war of 1960s and early 1970s, which left numerous bomb craters midst different groups of historic monuments. Only 71 structure ruins now survive. My Son ruins and shelled structures continue to provide archaeological evidence of rich cultural history, as well as exceptional artistic accomplishment of the Vietnamese people and trade networks in southeast Asia.

My Son site has spiritual roots in 1st–millennium Hinduism whose artistic interpretation evolved with Cham heritage and ideas. My Son sanctuary is located in the Duy Xuyen District of Quang Nam Province, in central Viet Nam. It is set within a valley surrounded by mountains, one of whom resembles the legendary Mount Meru and Kailasha. This is where the sacred Thu Bon river starts, then irrigates one of the heartland of Champa regions before meeting the South China Sea near famed historic port and economic center of Hoi An. My Son is the largest Champa site, whose history can be traced to the Dua people, who inspired by Hinduism, founded Champapura in late 2nd century (192 CE). These thereafter came to be known as Champa or Cham people. The oldest structures at My Son are from the 4th century. Over time, well over 100 Hindu shrines and structures were built here, mostly to the Shiva tradition – the Cham state religion, but also to Vishnu, Durga, Krishna and others. The site, at times, attracted syncretic Hindu-Mahayana Buddhist ideas. The My Son site is spread over miles, was predominantly built with bricks but one baked in such a way that appears to have been made from red sandstone. The monuments either face east or west. The site is archaeologically studied in many Nhoms (groups) – Group A ithrough Group M. Group B–C–D are together, built over 4th to 13th century near the confluence of two major river streams, and form the largest group of shrines. Group E–F are also together, dated to about the 7th-century, distinctive for the Vallabhi and Kalan architecture. Group A is the most magnificent structures built from 5th century onwards. Group G, H, L, M are isolated. Many of the isolated sites are rarely visited except by archaeologists and devout Cham pilgrims. The My Son site was in good state of preservation through the colonial era, as documented by a team led by the French architect and scholar Henri Parmentier. However, the site was badly damaged in the wars that followed, particularly the Vietnam war of 1960s and early 1970s, which left numerous bomb craters midst different groups of historic monuments. My Son ruins and shelled structures continue to provide archaeological evidence of rich cultural history, as well as exceptional artistic accomplishment of the Vietnamese people and cultural networks in southeast Asia.

file_title: File:A relatively large temple at My Son undergoes restoration (31801534195).jpg

captions.und: Having finished with the main cluster of ruins, we now head back out. On the way, near the exit, we come across this relatively large temple which is currently undergoing restoration. This entire region was a hotbed of Hinduism in it's glory days. What happened of all the Cham Hindus you ask? The descendants of the Champa Kingdom , numbering 400 000 - 1 million people live on the boarders of Cambodia and Viet Nam. Today they speak Cham or Cambodian (which they were forced to use after many were massacred by the Khmer Rouge). The Cham often live in villages of about 200 to 300 people. When the Champa Kingdom fell, the Cham who fled to Cambodia converted to Islam (and are now called Balamon or Utsuls). However, most Cham living in Viet Nam are Hindu (called Bani). (My Son, Central Vietnam, Nov. 2016)

L-19 042 at Zone 5 Military Museum, Danang
A Czechoslovak made 100 mm vz. 53 gun at the Zone 5 Military Museum (original: Bảo Tàng Khu 5) in Da Nang.

The building shown was originally built to serve as a gym and cafeteria, and was completed in January 1965. Before it could be opened for use, all dependents of U.S. government personnel in Vietnam were evacuated from the country and the school was closed for good. Three months later, the property became the home of the U.S. Army's 3rd Field Hospital, remaining such until 1973. The site was turned over then to the Saigon Adventist Hospital. In 1975, it was abandoned when military forces of North Vietnam captured Saigon. Here it is shown in its current use, as the 7th Military Zone Museum, a unit of the Army Military Museum of the People's Army of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. It is located at street address 247 Hoang Van Thu near the international airport for Ho Chi Minh City.

file_title: File:Catedral de San José, Hanoi, Vietnam (36400423110).jpg

captions.und: La Catedral de San José es una Catedral Católica, sede de la archidiócesis de Hanói. La iglesia fue construida en 1886 en el estilo neo-gótico durante la primera ocupación francesa de la ciudad, inspirada en Notre Dame de París. La iglesia es un lugar de reunión para la amplia comunidad católica de Hanói y también es una parada habitual de los turistas. Para construir la iglesia, los franceses derribaron la antigua pagoda Bao Thien, que ocupaba ese lugar desde hacía más de 800 años. El contraste entre los dos edificios religiosos era espectacular. La torre, la nave y la forma de cruz neogóticas de la catedral de San José son claramente europeos. Con sus 64,5 metros de longitud y los 31,5 metros de altura de sus campanarios, se trata de una estructura imponente. A la iglesia se accede por la puerta lateral y no por la entrada principal. En su interior, las ventanas con vidrieras y los murales religiosos conservan el estilo tradicional europeo del exterior. En cambio los pasillos, los muros y el altar están decorados con elementos de la tradición vietnamita. Durante muchos años no se celebraron los servicios por polémicas entre el Partido Comunista de Vietnam y el Vaticano, pero en 1990 se reinstauraron con mucho éxito. Se celebran oficios religiosos durante toda la semana y a menudo la iglesia se llena de fieles.

captions.und: A U.S. Navy Douglas A-4C Skyhawk launches from the aircraft carrier USS Enterprise (CVAN-65) in the Gulf of Tonkin on 13 May 1967. The Big E , with Carrier Air Wing 9 (CVW-9) embarked, was deployed to Vietnam from 19 November 1966 to 6 July 1967.

The U.S. nuclear-powered guided missile cruiser USS Long Beach (CGN-9) in the Gulf of Tonking, photographed between 24 March and 5 April 1967. The Long Beach was assigned to the PIRAZ (Positive Identification Radar Advisory Zone) station, controlling the flights over North Vietnam. A camouflaged SH-3A of HH-3A Sea King helicopter for combat search and rescue duties (nicknamed "Big Mother") is visible behind the aft Talos-launcher.

file_title: File:Dan Bevell demonstrates how to search underwater grid frame.png

captions.en: Staff Sgt. Dan Bevell, an Army diver assigned to the Defense POW/MIA Accountability Agency (DPAA), demonstrates how to search an underwater grid frame on a barge in the Gulf of Tonkin off the coast of Northern Vietnam, May 22, 2015. Bevell is part of an underwater recovery team searching for two aviators who are believed to have crashed in the area during the Vietnam War. Once the grid frame is secured to the ocean floor, divers from Mobile Diving and Salvage Unit ONE dredge inside the grid, and members of the joint recovery team sift through the dredged material in search of identifying evidence. (U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 1st Class Brett Cote/RELEASED)

Enjoy the sights, smells and thrills of Hanoi's Old Quarter on a self-propelled two-wheeler as you traverse through a 20km, four hour maze of side streets. Each tour is kept to a maximum of eight people and includes lunch. Urban Discovery also offers jaunts around Hanoi's West Lake and picturesque riverside. Discover Hanoi's wide boulevards and narrow alleyways on a bicycle tour with Urban Discovery. See: www.citypassguide.com

file_title: File:Crossing the Long Bien Bridge, Urban Discovery Tour, Hanoi (6914648592).jpg

captions.und: Long Biên Bridge (Cầu Long Biên) is an historic cantilever bridge across the Red River that connects two districts, Hoan Kiem and Long Bien of the city of Hanoi, Vietnam. The bridge was built in 1899-1902 by the architects Daydé & Pillé of Paris, and opened in 1903. Before North Vietnam's independence in 1954, it was called Paul-Doumer Bridge, named after Paul Doumer - The Governor-General of French Indochina and then French president. At 1.68 kilometres in length, it was, at that time, one of the longest bridges in Asia. For the French colonial government, the construction was of strategic importance in securing control of northern Vietnam. From 1899 to 1902, more than 3,000 Vietnamese took part in the construction. It was heavily bombarded during Vietnam War due to its critical position (the only bridge at that time across the Red River connecting Hanoi to the main port of Haiphong). The first attack took place in 1967, and the center span of the bridge was felled by an attack by 20 USAF F-105 fighter-bombers. CIA reports noted that the severing of the bridge did not appear to have caused as much disruption as had been expected. The defence of Long Bien Bridge continues to play a large role in Hanoi’s self-image and is often extolled in poetry and song. It was rendered unusable for a year when, in May 1972, it fell victim to one of the first co-ordinated attacks using laser-guided "smart bombs". captions.vi: Ai đi du lịch Hà Tiên, về thăm vùng đất Thập vịnh cảnh, có lẽ đều phải qua một vài khoảnh khắc miên man nghĩ, khi qua Cầu Tô Châu. Cây cầu này dài hơn 500m bắc qua sông Giang Thành mênh mông. Có thể nhiều người cũng đã từng nghe cái tên Sông Giang Thành, khi có dịp đi tour du lịch Hà Tiên Châu Đốc, song không phải ai cũng biết rõ về con sông này. Sông Gian Thành là một con sông khá nổi tiếng dài hơn 20km bắt nguồn từ Campuchia. Dòng chảy của nói đổ vào vũng Đông Hồ thuộc Hà Tiên rồi chảy ra Vịnh Thái Lan. Sông cũng nối với Kênh Vĩnh Tế của Châu Đốc, điểm giao nhau gọi là ngã ba Giang Thành, xưa được xem là một trong những cảnh đẹp của trấn Hà Tiên. Cũng chính ở khu vực này, Mạc Thiên Tứ đã cho đắp thành lũy đất dài gần 20km, kéo dài đến núi Châu Nham để bảo vệ bờ cõi khỏi quan xâm lăng. Ngày nay, dòng sông Giang Thành vẫn mênh mang một dòng chảy suốt và khi cầu Tô Châu được xây dựng, đã khiến cảnh quan như thêm hút hồn người. Cầu Tô Châu cũng trải qua một quá trình xây dựng dài, đến vài năm mới hoàn tất. Những vất vả đến cùng cũng được đáp trả xứng đáng vì nó tạo sự thuận lợi cho việc đi lại, và làm cho bức tranh phong cảnh Hà Tiên từ phía Giang Thành – Đông Hồ càng thêm quyến rũ hơn đến du khách xa gần mỗi khi có dịp ghé Hà Tiên. Cầu Tô Châu ra đời, không chỉ đảm đương một trách nhiệm quan trọng trong giao thông, mà còn đảm đương một sự kỳ vọng, niềm háo hức nối các bờ vui của du khách trong hành trình khám phá cảnh đẹp Hà Tiên, vốn xưa đã từng rất nổi tiếng. Đến thăm Hà Tiên, khi qua Cầu Tô Châu hầu như các công ty du lịch đều có những câu chuyện hay để kể về cây cầu này, như việc nó đã ra đời như thế nào, thay thế cho cầu phao ra sao để làm đường giao thông quan trọng giúp người người qua lại. Ở một góc độ khác của những người yêu cảnh quan thiên nhiên miền sông nước và yên mến Hà Tiên, lại như thấy thêm cây cầu này còn như một điểm dừng đầy sức hút, giúp cho lữ khách tìm được những khoảnh khắc miên man đầy hứng thú, trước cảnh đẹp giản dị nhưng bát ngát muôn trùng của sông nước Hà Tiên.

captions.und: La Cueva Paraíso (Paradise Cave o Hang Thien Duong) es una gruta situada en el parque nacional de Phong Nha-Ke Bang, en la provincia de Quang Binh, Vietnam. Ha sido designada Patrimonio de la Humanidad por la UNESCO. Fue descubierta en 2005 por una persona llamada Ho Khanh. Ese mismo año, un equipo de espeleólogos de la Asociación Británica para la investigación de Cuevas (British Cave Research Association) exploraron la cueva en su totalidad. Se trata de una cueva de origen kárstico de 31,4 km de largo, siendo la cueva "seca" más grande de Asia. Desde 2010 está abierta al público. Para la visita se ha habilitado un recorrido lineal de pasarelas de aproximadamente 1100 metros con un sistema de iluminación que realza las enormes formaciones de estalactitas y estalagmitas. Existen tours especiales que permiten adentrarse hasta 4,5 km en este mundo subterráneo. Para llegar a la entrada se debe ascender 570 metros por una pasarela entre la vegetación. Una vez que se ingresa, se debe bajar muchos escalones en la pasarela de madera para llegar a nivel del suelo. El comienzo de la cueva es una enorme caverna, más grande que un estadio de basketball, pero cuando se llega un poco más adentro son las estalactitas, las estalagmitas y las columnas de piedra caliza que dominan la vista. Las hay en todas las formas y tamaños diferentes -finas y gruesas, lisas y dentadas. Algunas parecen filas de guardianes vigilando su teatro, otras parecen casas, otras una cascada. Es difícil capturar en fotos la sensación de estar en Paradise Cave. Ninguna imagen puede mostrar la magnitud, los colores ni el detalle de esta maravilla creada por la naturaleza a través de 300 millones de años.

artist: Edgardo W. Olivera from Montevideo, Uruguay

captions.und: La Cueva Phong Nha (Phong Nha Cave) es una gruta situada en el parque nacional de Phong Nha-Ke Bang, en la provincia de Quang Binh, Vietnam. Tiene una longitud total de 7.729 metros, en los que se ubican unas catorce grutas. Por allí pasa un río subterráneo que tiene unos 13.969 metros de largo y aunque su serie de grutas tiene más de 44 metros de profundidad, los turistas solo pueden entrar un poco más de un kilómetro. Se agregó a la lista de sitios Patrimonio de la Humanidad en julio del 2003 por UNESCO. El pueblo Cham ha usado la cueva Phong Nha como un santuario budista en los siglos 9 y 10.

file_title: File:0040223 My Son UNESCO site entrance, Cham Hindu temples complex, Vietnam.jpg

captions.en: Mỹ Sơn is one of the largest historic, archaeological and cultural sites in southeast Asia. Now a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Vietnam , it served as a major religious and political center of the Champa Kingdom between the 4th and 14th centuries. My Son site has spiritual roots in 1st–millennium Hinduism whose artistic interpretation evolved with Cham heritage and ideas. My Son sanctuary is located in the Duy Xuyen District of Quang Nam Province, in central Viet Nam. It is set within a valley surrounded by mountains, one of whom resembles the legendary Mount Meru and Kailasha. This is where the sacred Thu Bon river starts, then irrigates one of the heartland of Champa regions before meeting the South China Sea near famed historic port and economic center of Hoi An. My Son is the largest Champa site, whose history can be traced to the Dua people, who inspired by Hinduism, founded Champapura in late 2nd century (192 CE). These thereafter came to be known as Champa or Cham people. The oldest structures at My Son are from the 4th century. Over time, well over 100 Hindu shrines and structures were built here, mostly to the Shiva tradition – the Cham state religion, but also to Vishnu, Durga, Krishna and others. The site, at times, attracted syncretic Hindu-Mahayana Buddhist ideas. The My Son site is spread over miles, was predominantly built with bricks but one baked in such a way that appears to have been made from red sandstone. The monuments either face east or west. The site is archaeologically studied in many Nhoms (groups) – Group A ithrough Group M. Group B–C–D are together, built over 4th to 13th century near the confluence of two major river streams, and form the largest group of shrines. Group E–F are also together, dated to about the 7th-century, distinctive for the Vallabhi and Kalan architecture. Group A is the most magnificent structures built from 5th century onwards. Group G, H, L, M are isolated. Many of the isolated sites are rarely visited except by archaeologists and devout Cham pilgrims. The My Son site was in good state of preservation through the colonial era, as documented by a team led by the French architect and scholar Henri Parmentier. However, the site was badly damaged in the wars that followed, particularly the Vietnam war of 1960s and early 1970s, which left numerous bomb craters midst different groups of historic monuments. My Son ruins and shelled structures continue to provide archaeological evidence of rich cultural history, as well as exceptional artistic accomplishment of the Vietnamese people and cultural networks in southeast Asia.

file_title: File:A far view of the ruins at My Son (30992152933).jpg

captions.und: We are now close to the My Son ruins complex. After getting off the bus, you still need to walk about half a km to the ruins themselves. So one km from the gate to the bus station, about three odd km on the bus, then half a km in- that should give you a fair idea as to how large the ruins complex is. Those are the My Son ruins in the distance. As you can see, many tourists, including the ones who left in two buses just ahead of us, are already there and are walking around. Notes about the My Son ruins appeared in one of the earlier captions, and will appear also in subsequent captions. (My Son, Central Vietnam, Nov. 2016)

file_title: File:Cueva Paraíso, Parque Nacional Phong Nha - Ke Bang, Vietnam (41309962172).jpg

captions.und: La Cueva Paraíso (Paradise Cave o Hang Thien Duong) es una gruta situada en el parque nacional de Phong Nha-Ke Bang, en la provincia de Quang Binh, Vietnam. Ha sido designada Patrimonio de la Humanidad por la UNESCO. Fue descubierta en 2005 por una persona llamada Ho Khanh. Ese mismo año, un equipo de espeleólogos de la Asociación Británica para la investigación de Cuevas (British Cave Research Association) exploraron la cueva en su totalidad. Se trata de una cueva de origen kárstico de 31,4 km de largo, siendo la cueva "seca" más grande de Asia. Desde 2010 está abierta al público. Para la visita se ha habilitado un recorrido lineal de pasarelas de aproximadamente 1100 metros con un sistema de iluminación que realza las enormes formaciones de estalactitas y estalagmitas. Existen tours especiales que permiten adentrarse hasta 4,5 km en este mundo subterráneo. Para llegar a la entrada se debe ascender 570 metros por una pasarela entre la vegetación. Una vez que se ingresa, se debe bajar muchos escalones en la pasarela de madera para llegar a nivel del suelo. El comienzo de la cueva es una enorme caverna, más grande que un estadio de basketball, pero cuando se llega un poco más adentro son las estalactitas, las estalagmitas y las columnas de piedra caliza que dominan la vista. Las hay en todas las formas y tamaños diferentes -finas y gruesas, lisas y dentadas. Algunas parecen filas de guardianes vigilando su teatro, otras parecen casas, otras una cascada. Es difícil capturar en fotos la sensación de estar en Paradise Cave. Ninguna imagen puede mostrar la magnitud, los colores ni el detalle de esta maravilla creada por la naturaleza a través de 300 millones de años.

file_title: File:Hùng miếu kỉ niệm bi (雄廟紀念碑).jpg

captions.vi: Hùng miếu kỉ niệm bi 雄廟紀念碑 Kí hiệu: 18707 Thác bản bia sưu tầm ở đền Hùng Vương xã Hi Cương tổng Xuân Lũng phủ Lâm Thao tỉnh Phú Thọ. Thác bản 1 mặt, khổ 80 x 130 cm, gồm 25 dòng chữ Hán, toàn văn ước khoảng 650 chữ, có hoa văn, không có chữ húy. Niên đại: Khải Định thứ 8 (1923). Người soạn: không ghi. Chủ đề: – Xây dựng, trùng tu di tích. Tóm lược nội dung: Về việc tu tạo miếu thờ vua Hùng. Từ năm Tự Đức phụng sắc trùng tu, lập bia đá ghi chép về việc đó. Đến năm Duy Tân thứ 3 mới lại hưng công tu tạo. Từ đó đến nay trải các lần được cấp tiền để trùng tu đều có hội đồng quản cố. Nay lập bia ghi chép lại vào các năm, tu tạo các khoản gì, những người tán thành chủ trương…

captions.en: (READ THE THIRD PICTURE FOR A SURPRISE ENDING) - the red sign is Happy New Year The splendid mausoleum of Emperor Tu Duc (1848-1883) (a Nguyen Emperor). Built between 1864 and 1867, is perhaps the most exquisitely designed of the Nguyen mausoleums. It's built on a grand scale, but with a perfect eye for detail. Designed by Tu Duc himself, the mausoleum is set amidst fragrant pines and frangipani trees, surrounded by tranquil, lotus-filled waters. The emperor spent a lot of time here during the tomb's three years of construction. It was Tu Duc's habit to recline here in the gorgeous Xung Khiem Pavilion composing poetry and reflecting--one might suspect--on the transience of mundane existence. A lovely place indeed, but not without its dark side. When Tu Duc expired he was buried secretly, reputedly with great treasure. Reportedly all 200 of the servants involved in the burial were subsequently beheaded to keep the Emperor's final resting-place hidden from tomb robbers and safe from desecration! Hue, Vietnam

Luu Khiem Lake and Tinh Khiem Island. The lake was created from a small stream once running through the tomb area. The excavated earth was used to construct the island. The building is the Xung Khiem Pavilion where the Emperor spent a lot of time. Hue, Vietnam

captions.und: Cour d'honneur avec les gardes et à droite le pavillon de la Stèle. Monté sur le trône du Vietnam en 1916, le roi Khai Dinh choisit la pente de la montagne Chau Chu (encore appelée Chau E), à 10 km de Huê, pour y bâtir son tombeau. Les travaux commencèrent le 4 septembre 1920 et se poursuivirent pendant 11 ans. Le roi étant mort en 1925, le tombeau a été terminé sous Bao Dai (1926-1945). Le tombeau est le résultat du mélange des architectures européennes et asiatiques, modernes et anciennes. Il est divisé, comme le veut la tradition, en 3 parties qui dans ce cas sont des terrasses reliées par des escaliers. La première terrasse est bordée de pavillons de garde. La deuxième terrasse comprend la cour d'honneur, des soldats, animaux et mandarins et le pavillon de la Stèle sur laquelle sont inscrits les réalisations et mérites du roi. La troisième terrasse est celle du tombeau et des salles commémoratives décorées de mosaïques, faïences et tessons de verre.

captions.und: The Presidential Palace of Vietnam, located in the city of Hanoi, was built between 1900 and 1906 to house the French Governor-General of Indochina. It was constructed by Auguste Henri Vildieu, the official French architect for Vietnam. Like most French colonial architecture, the palace is pointedly European- the only visual cues that it is located in Vietnam at all are mango trees growing on the grounds. The striking yellow palace stands behind wrought iron gates flanked by sentry boxes. It incorporates elements of Italian Renaissance design, including: * aedicules * a formal piano nobile reached by a grand staircase * broken pediments * classical columns * quoins When Vietnam achieved independence in 1954, Ho Chi Minh refused to live in the grand structure for symbolic reasons, although he still received state guests there, and he eventually built a traditional Vietnamese stilt house and carp pond on the grounds. Today, Ho Chi Minh's Mausoleum stands nearby and the Presidential Palace remains part of Hanoi's cultural core. The palace hosts government meetings. It is not open to the public, although one may walk around the grounds for a fee. [Wikipedia.org]

captions.en: Mountains in ocean, Lan Hạ Bay, Vietnam.

captions.und: Ningún viaje al norte de Vietnam puede ser considerado completo sin una visita a la región de la bahía de Halong. Esta región en realidad incluye 3 bahías: Bai Tu Long, Lan Ha y por último pero no menos importante, la bahía de Halong. Halong Bay es la más conocida por los turistas que vienen de todo el mundo. Sin embargo, Lan Ha Bay y Bai Tu Long Bay tienen la misma belleza escénica que Bahía de Halong, o más. No muchos visitantes extranjeros son conscientes de que las formaciones rocosas e islas van más allá del "Ha Long Bay Park". Desde un punto administrativo representan tres parques separados, cada uno con sus propias tarifas turísticas, pero desde un punto de vista geológico y geográfico, son tratadas como un todo. Menos turística que su hermana mayor (Halong) pero no menos increíble, Lan Ha Bay es una hermosa bahía llena de islas y rocas, donde se pueden apreciar pueblos flotantes de pescadores y cultivadores de mariscos. Situada al sur y al este de la ciudad de Cat Ba, las 300 o más islas kársticas y de piedra caliza de Lan Ha son tan hermosas como las de la bahía de Halong y tienen la atracción adicional de numerosas playas de arena blanca. Geológicamente, Lan Ha es una extensión de la Bahía de Halong, pero se encuentra en una provincia diferente. Alrededor de 200 especies de peces, 500 especies de moluscos, 400 especies de artrópodos, y numerosos corales duros y blandos viven en sus aguas, mientras que los animales marinos más grandes de la zona incluyen focas y tres especies de delfines.

Not the biggest in the region, nonetheless the floating market at Cai Be was bustling with activity as boats came and went and traded and swapped loads of fresh fruits and vegetables grown in nearby fields and orchards. captions.und: Cette maison a été construite en bois au XIXe siècle au bord du Mékong par M. Phan Dang Van. En 1938, à l'époque coloniale, elle a été reconstruite et entourée d'un vaste parc (arbres fruitiers et arbres d'ornement). Le style colonial de la maison est unique, car il associe des caractères français et vietnamiens. L'habitation a été surélevée pour éviter d'être inondée lors des crues du Mékong, pendant la mousson. La maison est divisée en deux parties séparées par une cour intérieure. La partie avant sert à la réception des visiteurs et abrite l'autel des ancêtres. Elle est meublée de façon traditionnelle comme à l'origine. La plupart des meubles datent de la fin du 19e et du début du 20e siècle. Au milieu de la pièce principale, quatre ensembles de piliers en Xylia xylocarpa “cam xe” renforcent la stabilité de l'édifice. Des panneaux en bois d'ébène, accrochés aux piliers, sont incrustés de caractères vietnamiens anciens en nacre. Ces inscriptions ont pour but de rappeler les valeurs fondamentales des fondateurs : faire le bien et avoir de la compassion pour les autres. A l'arrière de la maison historique, une maison a été aménagée pour accueillir des voyageurs intéressés par l'écotourisme. site du propriétaire www.bacdumekong.com

file_title: File:La pagode Tay An (Chau Doc, Vietnam) (6620545789).jpg

captions.und: L'entrée de la pagode Tay An (Bouddhisme mahāyāna, Grand Véhicule) La pagode Tay An (Chua Tay An) a été fondée en 1847, refaite en 1861, et reconstruite en 1958. Elle est située au pied du Mont Sam. A l'image des multiples communautés habitant cette région, son architecture très colorée traduit des influences hindoues, vietnamiennes bouddhistes et islamistes. Elle contient de nombreuses statuettes et statues, dont un grand nombre est en bois. On y trouve de nombreux Bouddhas, l'Empereur de Jade, les Arhats, les quatre Rois célestes, les gardiens du Dharma, des représentations de génies locaux.

captions.vi: Thác Đăng Mò thuộc địa phận huyện Bình Gia, tỉnh Lạng Sơn, quanh năm đổ tràn qua những triền đá giữa núi rừng hoang sơ, mang vẻ đẹp vô cùng nên thơ và huyền bí. Cách thành phố Lạng Sơn khoảng 90 km, Thác Đăng Mò nằm ở vị trí cây số 11 trên đường quốc lộ 279 từ huyện Bình Gia tỉnh Lạng Sơn đi huyện Na Rì tỉnh Bắc Kạn, là nơi tiếp giáp của ba xã vùng cao của huyện Bình Gia: Mông Ân, Thiện thuật, và xã Hoàng Văn Thụ.
